episode.title: The Night Shift
episode.subtitle: A bounded, synthetic evidence-discovery episode
episode.opening: A 61-year-old arrives with sudden severe chest discomfort. The team is already arranging urgent assessment. The initial handoff is incomplete.
episode.disclaimer: Educational game only. All measurements and events in this investigation are authored fictional content pending human review, not clinical advice or source facts.

sources.title: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease

actions.label: Build the symptom timeline
actions.finding: Authored fictional history: abrupt chest pain was maximal at onset and moved through to the back.
actions.interpretation: The onset and radiation are high-risk features, but they do not identify one diagnosis by themselves.

actions.label: Perform a focused examination
actions.finding: Authored fictional measurement: arm pressures are 178/105 on the right and 142/88 on the left; the difference is reproducible.
actions.interpretation: The fictional inter-arm difference increases concern for an aortic process and keeps premature coronary anchoring unsafe.

actions.label: Review the ECG
actions.finding: Authored fictional tracing: a small, nonspecific ST change is present in aVL without a complete diagnostic pattern.
actions.interpretation: This finding keeps acute coronary syndrome in the differential but is not decisive and cannot erase the aortic warning signs.

actions.label: Review the chest radiograph
actions.finding: Authored fictional radiograph: the mediastinal contour is described as subtly widened, with no single definitive answer.
actions.interpretation: A plain chest radiograph cannot exclude acute aortic syndrome; this fictional image is an ambiguity-preserving clue, not a diagnosis.

actions.label: Obtain CT angiography of the aorta
actions.finding: Authored fictional CTA report: an intimal flap is seen in the ascending aorta and extends into the arch.
actions.interpretation: In this fictional episode, the CTA is the decisive clue favoring acute aortic syndrome over the competing hypotheses.

actions.label: Make a specialist handoff
actions.finding: The fictional handoff carries the symptom report and CTA finding; it does not imply that other observations were performed.
actions.interpretation: A structured handoff preserves uncertainty and the decisive clue for human review; it does not model treatment or outcome.

openingFacts.label: Sudden severe chest discomfort in the opening handoff

uncertaintyOptions.label: The opening symptom does not identify one cause.
The nonspecific ECG finding does not settle the cause.
The CTA supports an aortic finding; it does not settle every aspect of care.
Every competing explanation has now been excluded.

transfer.prompt: A different fictional patient has sudden severe chest pain. The CTA report says motion obscures the ascending aorta and calls that segment nondiagnostic. No definite flap is reported. Which conclusion best respects this evidence?

choices.label: The absence of a reported flap excludes an aortic process.
choices.feedback: A nondiagnostic segment is not a reliable negative finding. The report explicitly limits what can be concluded.

choices.label: The aortic question remains unresolved; the team needs to clarify the inadequate study.
choices.feedback: The limitation matters. Image acquisition and motion affect diagnostic confidence, so an inadequate segment cannot carry an exclusion claim.

choices.label: The symptom pattern alone confirms dissection despite the report.
choices.feedback: The symptoms justify concern, not certainty. The fictional report has not established the diagnosis.

source.title: 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline: CT image quality

episode.title: The Missed Turn
episode.subtitle: A sudden interruption. An incomplete picture.
episode.opening: At dinner, a 68-year-old suddenly cannot finish a sentence and has trouble holding a fork. Emergency help is already on the way. Follow the fictional team record as it arrives.
episode.disclaimer: Educational game only. All measurements, reports and events are authored fiction pending human review, not clinical advice or source facts.

presentation.imageAlt: Generated illustration of a dinner interrupted by an emergency response. Not diagnostic evidence.

sources.title: NICE NG128: stroke recognition and initial assessment, recommendations 1.1.1-1.1.3
sources.scope: Sudden focal symptoms and checking hypoglycaemia as a competing explanation. The fictional normal glucose weakens that rival without establishing stroke; no treatment content is used.

sources.title: NINDS: Assess and Treat, CT and MRI sections
sources.scope: CT detects bleeding; diffusion MRI can show ischemia before a non-contrast CT. Supports limits of the authored reports, not a required scan sequence or patient-specific advice.

actions.label: Ask what changed at dinner
actions.finding: Fictional witness account: speech was normal a moment earlier. Word-finding difficulty and right-hand weakness began together and persist.
actions.interpretation: Sudden speech and one-sided movement changes call for urgent assessment, not a wait-and-see conclusion.

actions.label: Read the team examination
actions.finding: Fictional examination: the clinician records difficulty naming familiar objects and right-arm drift. The patient remains awake.
actions.interpretation: The observed pattern strengthens concern but does not establish its cause alone.

actions.label: Read the blood glucose result
actions.finding: Fictional measurement during the symptoms: blood glucose is 106 mg/dL (5.9 mmol/L).
actions.interpretation: This result does not support low glucose as the current explanation; it does not itself prove stroke.

actions.label: Read the first scan report
actions.finding: Fictional non-contrast head CT report: no hemorrhage is seen; no definite early infarct is visible.
actions.interpretation: An early CT without a visible infarct does not rule out ischemic stroke.

actions.label: Read the later imaging review
actions.finding: Fictional team review: diffusion MRI shows a small acute left frontal infarct corresponding to the speech and right-arm changes.
actions.interpretation: The matching imaging finding supports ischemic stroke in this authored story; it is not a rule that every suspected stroke needs MRI before action.

actions.label: Pass on the witness account
actions.finding: The fictional handoff preserves the witnessed onset and persisting changes. It makes no claim about examinations or scans you did not read.
actions.interpretation: A useful handoff separates what was witnessed from what remains unknown.

reasoning.limitationLabel: Compare explanations or identify a limit
reasoning.prompt: Explain how a finding you read supports your concern, how the alternatives compare, and what the record still cannot establish.
reasoning.caseLearningText: Weakening one explanation does not prove another. Connect each collected finding to the concern it supports or weakens, and keep a working hypothesis provisional when decisive evidence is absent.
reasoning.insufficientCitationFeedback: Your route includes the matching fictional imaging finding. Cite that finding to support the conclusion rather than an earlier concern or a result that only weakens a rival.

openingFacts.label: Sudden speech and hand-use changes in the opening handoff

glucose-result.conflictFeedback: The glucose result you read during the symptoms does not support low glucose as the current explanation. It weakens that rival without proving ischemic stroke.

uncertaintyOptions.label: The opening symptoms raise concern but do not establish a cause.
The glucose result weakens the low-glucose explanation; it is not a positive stroke test.
The first CT report does not exclude an early ischemic stroke.
The matching MRI finding supports ischemic stroke here; it does not determine every cause or later care decision.
Every competing cause has now been ruled out.

resolution.supportedSummary: Your conclusion fits the matching acute infarct described in the fictional imaging review. This is support from that recorded finding, beyond the opening symptoms alone.
resolution.mismatchSummary: The chosen explanation does not account for the matching acute infarct described in the fictional imaging review.
resolution.provisionalSummary: Your route ended before the later imaging review. The conclusion remains provisional; a working hypothesis is not confirmation.
resolution.decisiveClue: The later fictional MRI report describes an acute left frontal infarct matching the symptoms.
resolution.missingClue: The later imaging review was not collected. No decisive imaging clue was reached on this route.
resolution.nextLearning: Distinguish a test that finds no bleeding from evidence that excludes interrupted blood flow. Keep uncertainty visible.
limitations: Synthetic preview pending human medical review. This is a reasoning exercise, not a validated diagnostic assessment.
Reports are fictional text, not scans. Scene art is reused illustration, not a patient record or diagnostic evidence.
Timing is authored, non-real-time and non-prognostic. Reading order does not prescribe a clinical workup. Emergency assessment continues independently of your choices.

transfer.prompt: In another fictional story, sudden trouble speaking and one-sided weakness disappear after ten minutes. Emergency help has already been called. What changes about the concern?

choices.label: Because the symptoms stopped, urgent assessment is no longer needed.
choices.feedback: Improvement does not remove the concern. Brief neurological symptoms can still represent an important warning event.

choices.label: The duration proves that a completed stroke occurred.
choices.feedback: Duration alone cannot establish the cause. The team still needs to assess what happened.

choices.label: The cause remains uncertain, and urgent professional assessment still matters.
choices.feedback: The uncertainty and urgency coexist. NICE calls for immediate referral for suspected TIA, with specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset.

episode.title: After the Weekend
episode.subtitle: A familiar complaint. Three pieces that must fit.
episode.opening: A 26-year-old arrives after a weekend away with vomiting, fatigue and abdominal discomfort. The team is already assessing the patient. The first handoff suggests a stomach illness, but the record is incomplete.
episode.disclaimer: Educational game only. All measurements, reports and events are authored fiction pending human review, not clinical advice or source facts.

presentation.imageAlt: Generated illustration of a young adult under observation with a hospital team. Not diagnostic evidence.

sources.title: ADA/EASD and partner societies: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes, 2024 consensus report
sources.scope: Diagnosis requires the combined glucose/diabetes, ketone and metabolic-acidosis criteria. HHS involves hyperosmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis; no treatment recommendations are used. Fictional values are not source patient data.

sources.title: 2024 consensus report: open full text, diagnostic criteria section
sources.scope: Primary consensus text for the three-part DKA argument and the competing HHS pattern. Used only to check authored evidence relations, not care decisions.

actions.label: Clarify the recent history
actions.finding: Fictional history: thirst and frequent urination started before the vomiting. There is no established diabetes diagnosis in the record.
actions.interpretation: The chronology weakens a stomach-only explanation but cannot settle the metabolic diagnosis.

actions.label: Read the bedside observations
actions.finding: Fictional observations: the patient is tired but conversant, with deep breathing, dry mouth and diffuse abdominal discomfort.
actions.interpretation: These observations require explanation; they are not specific enough to label the illness.

actions.label: Review the plasma glucose
actions.finding: Fictional laboratory result: plasma glucose is 286 mg/dL.
actions.interpretation: Elevated glucose alone is not sufficient to establish ketoacidosis.

actions.label: Review the blood ketones
actions.finding: Fictional laboratory result: beta-hydroxybutyrate is 4.8 mmol/L.
actions.interpretation: The ketone result adds a second piece. Acid-base evidence is still distinct.

actions.label: Review the acid-base results
actions.finding: Fictional laboratory results: venous pH is 7.22 and bicarbonate is 13 mmol/L.
actions.interpretation: Acidosis together with elevated glucose and ketones supports the ketoacidosis explanation in this case.

actions.label: Review serum osmolality
actions.finding: Fictional laboratory result: measured total serum osmolality is 297 mOsm/kg.
actions.interpretation: This fictional result does not support a markedly hyperosmolar explanation. It does not replace the three-part ketoacidosis assessment.

reasoning.limitationLabel: Compare explanations or identify a limit
reasoning.prompt: Choose a relevant fact or the combined glucose, ketone and acid-base argument. Explain what it supports, how the alternatives compare, and what remains uncertain.
reasoning.caseLearningText: Keep glucose, ketones and acid-base evidence distinct until you can connect them. Compare the metabolic explanation with its rivals; one abnormal result is not the whole argument. These alternatives are simplified; real presentations can overlap.
reasoning.insufficientCitationFeedback: The three-part argument needs the glucose, ketone and acid-base findings together. Select their combined argument to justify this conclusion; citing one component does not demonstrate that connection.

openingFacts.label: Vomiting, fatigue and abdominal discomfort in the opening handoff

plasma-glucose.conflictFeedback: The glucose value you read does not fit HHS alone in this fictional case. It does not establish DKA without the remaining findings; real presentations can overlap.

blood-ketones.conflictFeedback: The ketone elevation you read does not fit HHS alone in this fictional case. It does not establish DKA without the remaining findings; real presentations can overlap.

acid-base.conflictFeedback: The acidosis you read does not fit HHS alone in this fictional case. It does not establish DKA without the remaining findings; real presentations can overlap.

serum-osmolality.conflictFeedback: The osmolality result you read does not support HHS alone in this fictional case. It does not establish DKA without the remaining findings; real presentations can overlap.

supportGroups.label: Glucose, blood ketones and acid-base results together

uncertaintyOptions.label: Vomiting and discomfort alone do not establish a metabolic diagnosis.
Thirst and frequent urination before vomiting weaken a stomach-only explanation; the metabolic cause is still unresolved.
Glucose is raised, but a ketone or acid-base report is still missing from my route.
Ketones are raised, but a glucose or acid-base report is still missing from my route.
A glucose or ketone report is still missing, so this acidosis has not been linked to the full pattern.
The laboratory pattern supports ketoacidosis here; it does not determine why it developed or settle every care decision.
This osmolality result weakens a markedly hyperosmolar explanation; it cannot establish ketoacidosis on its own.
Every other cause of vomiting has now been ruled out.

resolution.supportedSummary: The collected three-part pattern supports ketoacidosis in this fictional case: elevated glucose, ketones and acidosis. The opening complaint alone was not enough.
resolution.mismatchSummary: The collected glucose, ketone and acid-base findings fit ketoacidosis more closely than the selected explanation in this fictional case.
resolution.provisionalSummary: Your conclusion remains provisional because the glucose, ketone and acid-base results were not all collected. A partial pattern is not the complete evidence set.
resolution.decisiveClue: The fictional combination is glucose 286 mg/dL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.8 mmol/L, pH 7.22 and bicarbonate 13 mmol/L.
resolution.missingClue: At least one component of the three-part laboratory pattern is missing from your route.
resolution.nextLearning: Ask whether the required pieces fit together, rather than letting one abnormal number carry the whole conclusion.

transfer.prompt: A different fictional patient has dehydration, glucose 720 mg/dL, measured total osmolality 334 mOsm/kg, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36 and bicarbonate 23 mmol/L. Which explanation fits this laboratory pattern better?

choices.label: Ketoacidosis, because any very high glucose is sufficient.
choices.feedback: High glucose alone does not establish ketoacidosis. The marked ketosis and acidosis from the earlier case are absent here.

choices.label: A hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state rather than the earlier ketoacidotic pattern.
choices.feedback: This authored pattern combines severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketosis or acidosis. It contrasts with the three-part ketoacidosis pattern.

choices.label: No major metabolic problem, because the pH is not low.
choices.feedback: A near-normal pH does not make severe hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality harmless. The full pattern matters.
